Theme

Latin word

scientia

scientia, scientiae f.

noun, first declension · Declension on Wiktionary

knowledge (of a subject), knowing; science; the systematic knowledge of a field; knowledge without practice

In this lexicon

  • knowledge

    the recommended word · classical · Cic. Off. 1.18: ad cognitiōnis et scientiae cupiditātem; Caes. BG 3.8.1: scientiā atque ūsū rērum nauticārum; Traupman 337, 155

  • science

    the recommended word · classical · Cic. Fin. 1.63: In physicīs plūrimum posuit. eā scientiā …; Vitr. 3 praef. 1: disciplīnārum scientiae; M-O s.v. science (natural sciences): scientia nātūrālis, after Pallas (1811)

  • theory

    also used · classical · Cic. Rep. 1.2: scientiā tamen ipsā tenērī potest

  • māchinālis scientia, māchinālis scientiae f.: engineer

    classical

  • Ipsa scientia potestās est.: knowledge is power

    Renaissance

Examples

  • Omnēs enim trahimur et dūcimur ad cognitiōnis et scientiae cupiditātem, in quā excellere pulchrum putāmus

    for we are all drawn and led to the desire for learning and knowledge, and we think it a fine thing to excel in itCic. Off. 1.18

    In the entry for knowledge

  • sed est ūnum perfugium doctrīna ac litterae, quibus semper ūsī sumus

    but there is one refuge, learning and books, which we have always made use ofCic. Fam. 6.12.5

    In the entry for knowledge

  • In physicīs plūrimum posuit. … omnium autem rērum nātūrā cognitā levāmur superstitiōne, līberāmur mortis metū

    He set the greatest store by natural science. … Once we know the nature of all things, we are freed from superstition and from the fear of deathCic. Fin. 1.63

    In the entry for science

  • physicum, id est speculātōrem vēnātōremque nātūrae

    a scientist, that is, an observer and hunter of natureCic. ND 1.83

    In the entry for science

  • Nec vērō habēre virtūtem satis est quasi artem aliquam, nisi ūtāre; etsī ars quidem, cum eā nōn ūtāre, scientiā tamen ipsā tenērī potest, virtūs in ūsū suī tōta posita est

    Nor is it enough to have virtue as one has some art, unless you use it; for an art, even when you do not use it, can still be held by knowledge alone, but virtue lies wholly in its useCic. Rep. 1.2
